title: Normal multiplicative-type layers in a connected group are central
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. A group is of multiplicative type if, after extension to an algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], it admits a closed group immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] into $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$ [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type, def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be connected [def-weil-connected-scheme], and let $N\subseteq E\subseteq G$ be subgroups both normal in $G$. Let $q:E\to Q$ represent the fppf quotient $E/N$: its represented sheaf is the sheafification of $A\mapsto E(A)/N(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]. Assume $N$ and $Q$ are of multiplicative type. Then $E$ is of multiplicative type and $E\subseteq Z(G)$ [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change]. Explicitly, for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, every $e\in E(A)$ and every commutative $A$-algebra $A^{\prime}$, the image of $e$ commutes with all of $G(A^{\prime})$. No smoothness, perfectness, or connectedness of $N,E,Q$ is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 16.43, printed p.340. Corollary 12.38, p.244, first makes N central in G (hence in E), so the central-kernel correction to Corollary 12.41 in the Chapter 12 erratum is satisfied; Corollary 12.22, p.239, gives multiplicative type after commutativity.

proof.text: Put $R=k[Q]$ and $S=k[E]$. By the quotient hypothesis, $q$ is flat and surjective and $N=\ker q$. The affine flatness criterion makes $R\to S$ flat; surjectivity of its spectrum then makes it faithfully flat. The affine fibre-product formula and preservation of faithful flatness under ring base change show that every pullback of $q$ to an affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}B\to Q$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_R S)\to\operatorname{Spec}B$, flat and surjective. In particular the inverse image of every affine open of $Q$ is affine and surjects onto that open. Thus $q$ is an fpqc cover by the definition. We may pull this cover back and compose such covers; in particular products with the parameter group and products of two copies of $q$ are fpqc covers. For the latter, factor $1\times q\times q$ as $1\times q\times1$ followed by $1\times1\times q$.

source.place: Tag 022D, lemma-fpqc; affine criterion Tag 01U5, morphisms.tex lemma-flat-characterize, and faithful-flat spectrum criterion Tag 00HQ, algebra.tex lemma-ff-rings. This supplies the quotient-cover details for Milne 16.43.

proof.text: Set $F=\bar k$ and append a subscript $F$ to scalar extensions. The identity gives a $k$-rational point of $G$, whose residue field is $k$; the connected-point geometric-connectedness criterion therefore makes $G_F$ connected. The affine fibre-product formula identifies the new coordinate rings with $F\otimes_k k[H]$ for $H=G,E,N,Q$. Group operations, inclusions, normality and the kernel identity pull back by the fibre-product definition: on an $F$-algebra they are the original operations and kernel tested on its underlying $k$-algebra. Closedness persists because tensoring a surjective presentation remains surjective (lift the finitely many coefficients of each tensor); finite generation persists by the same generators. The map $q_F$ is an fpqc cover by step 1, and its coordinate map is faithfully flat by ring base change. The multiplicative-type hypotheses give closed immersions of $N_F,Q_F$ into split tori. The split-torus subgroup theorem thus writes each as $D(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ with $M$ finitely generated abelian. Work over $F$ in steps 3--7, suppressing subscripts.

source.place: Lemma 16.43, p.340, reduction to an algebraic closure; Stacks Tag 04KV, varieties.tex lemma-geometrically-connected-if-connected-and-point. Diagonalizability is Milne Theorem 12.9(c), p.233.

proof.text: Normality of $N$ in $G$ restricts conjugation to $\phi:G\times_F N\to N$. For every $F$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$, this is the group automorphism $n\mapsto gng^{-1}$, with inverse conjugation by $g^{-1}$. Apply homomorphism-family rigidity with $X=G$, $x_0=1_G$, and $D_1=D_2=N$. Step 2 supplies a connected affine finite-type parameter scheme and a diagonalizable target and source; the lemma requires no smoothness. At $x_0$ conjugation is the identity, hence $gng^{-1}=n$ on every algebra. Thus $N$ is central in $G$, in particular central in $E$. This proves the extra hypothesis required by the Chapter 12 correction before it is used.

source.place: Corollary 12.38, p.244, obtained directly from Theorem 12.36, pp.243--244; Chapter 12 erratum: the kernel in Corollary 12.41 must be central.

proof.text: Write $a(g,e)=geg^{-1}$, a morphism $G\times_F E\to E$ because $E$ is normal in $G$; it preserves $N$. Descend $q\circ a$ along $p=1_G\times q$. Its overlap is $G\times_F E\times_F N$, with two lifts $e,en$: the kernel-pair isomorphism sends $(e,n)$ to $(e,en)$ and its inverse sends $(e,e')$ to $(e,e^{-1}e')$. On the overlap, $q(a(g,en))=q(a(g,e)a(g,n))=q(a(g,e))$, since $a(g,n)\in N$. Representable fpqc descent gives a morphism $b:G\times_F Q\to Q$ satisfying $b(g,q(e))=q(a(g,e))$. It is over $F$, since its structure maps agree after the cover. Its homomorphism identity in the second variable holds: after the product cover by $G\times_F E\times_F E$, it reads $q(a(g,ee'))=q(a(g,e))q(a(g,e'))$; uniqueness in descent proves the original identity. Likewise $b(g,1)=1$ and $b(1,t)=t$ follow after $p$ or $q$ from the corresponding identities of $a$. Homomorphism-family rigidity with $X=G$, $x_0=1_G$, $D_1=D_2=Q$ now gives $b(g,t)=t$. Thus $q(a(g,e))=q(e)$.

source.place: Proof of corrected Corollary 12.41, p.244, quotient action and Corollary 12.37 via Theorem 12.36; representable descent is Stacks Tag 023Q, descent.tex lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms.

proof.text:
Define $c(g,e)=a(g,e)e^{-1}$. Step 4 gives $q(c(g,e))=1$, so the kernel fibre product makes $c$ a morphism to $N$. On the overlap from step 4, step 3 gives
$$c(g,en)=a(g,e)n(en)^{-1}=c(g,e).$$
Descent therefore yields $d:G\times_F Q\to N$ with $d(g,q(e))=c(g,e)$. Centrality of $N$ in $E$ proves, on every algebra,
$$c(g,ee')=a(g,e)a(g,e')e'^{-1}e^{-1}=c(g,e)e\,c(g,e')e^{-1}=c(g,e)c(g,e').$$
Also $c(g,1)=1$. Pulling back along the product cover $G\times_F E\times_F E\to G\times_F Q\times_F Q$ and using uniqueness in descent proves that $d(g,-)$ is a homomorphism; the unit equality descends in the same way. Finally $d(1_G,-)=1$, since this holds after $q$. Thus it is the difference $c$, rather than $a$ itself, which descends to a family $Q\to N$.

source.place: Proof of corrected Corollary 12.41, p.244, two factorizations interpreted for the difference a(g,e)e^{-1}; central-kernel Chapter 12 erratum. Descent is Stacks Tag 023Q, descent.tex lemma-fpqc-universal-effective-epimorphisms.

proof.text: Apply homomorphism-family rigidity to $d$ with $X=G$, $x_0=1_G$, $D_1=Q$, $D_2=N$. Both diagonalizable groups were obtained in step 2, and step 5 proves the family-of-homomorphisms hypothesis. Hence $d(g,t)=d(1_G,t)=1$, so $a(g,e)e^{-1}=1$. Therefore conjugation $G\times_F E\to E$ is the second projection. In particular the multiplication of $E$ is commutative. These are morphism identities, not merely identities at $F$-points: the rigidity lemma tests every algebra, and evaluating at the coordinate algebra of the affine source identifies its two comorphisms.

source.place: Theorem 12.36, pp.243--244, and Lemma 16.43, p.340: trivial conjugation gives centrality and commutativity.

proof.text: The coordinate map of $q$ is faithfully flat by steps 1--2; its kernel is $N$, and $N,Q$ are diagonalizable. Apply the commutative multiplicative-type extension lemma to the commutative $E$ from step 6. It gives $E\simeq D(M)$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$. To recover precisely the immersion formulation in the item, choose generators $m_1,\ldots,m_r$ of $M$. The map $F[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]\to F[M]$ sending $t_i$ to $e_{m_i}$ is surjective: every basis element $e_m$ is a Laurent monomial in these generators. It preserves the group operations since each $e_{m_i}$ is group-like. Its spectrum is consequently a closed group immersion of $E$ into $\mathbf G_m^r$. This proves that the original $E$ is of multiplicative type by its defining condition over $\bar k$.

source.place: Corollary 12.22, p.239, as used in Lemma 16.43, p.340; the closed immersion from finitely many character generators is the construction in Theorem 12.9, pp.233--234.

proof.text: Restore the original field $k$. Let $a:G\times_k E\to G$ be conjugation followed by inclusion, and let $j\operatorname{pr}_E:G\times_k E\to G$ be projection followed by inclusion. Step 6 says their scalar extensions to $F$ agree. For each $f\in k[G]$, the difference of their pullbacks in $B=k[G\times_k E]$ has zero image in $B\otimes_k F$ by the affine fibre-product formula. The field-extension tensor-injectivity lemma forces that difference to be zero. The affine spectrum correspondence gives $a=j\operatorname{pr}_E$ over $k$. For any $k$-algebra $A$, $e\in E(A)$ and $A$-algebra $A'$, evaluating this equality at $(g,e_{A'})$ for every $g\in G(A')$ gives $ge_{A'}g^{-1}=e_{A'}$. This is exactly the defining functor of $Z(G)$ in the cited centre lemma, so $E\subseteq Z(G)$ with the explicit all-algebras meaning required.
